We present photometric observations of the binary companions to the luminous blue variables (LBVs) SN 1987A and SN 1967G. We show that these systems contain extremely close pairs of white dwarfs in wide (8–9 days) orbit around the blue dwarf. The mass of the blue dwarf is not much greater than the mass of the white dwarf in either system. Thus, these systems are not useful for studying the evolution of field LBVs. The close white dwarf pairs are unusual and of interest in their own right, however. We discuss the possibility that the evolution of these systems has been influenced by the exchange of material between the two stars, possibly leading to the white dwarf's acquiring a significant fraction of its current mass. The accretion history of the white dwarf is probably not unique, so this may provide a mechanism for the evolution of other field LBVs. The low-mass objects in these systems may be the first examples of objects in the so-called detached object category that has been proposed as a possible route to the evolution of type I supernovae.

We have discovered a new detached binary in the planetary nebula around SN 1987A. The binary is composed of an orbital pair of white dwarfs in a widely asymmetric (80-day) orbit around a blue dwarf. The blue dwarf is slightly more massive than the white dwarfs. This is the third detached binary discovered in the last year, providing support for the hypothesis that these objects are an important stage in the evolution of massive binary systems.

However your attempt may look, don't panic. Right click on each blue side, select Erase and it will be gone. Click on the Eraser tool and get rid of the lines demonstrated in the screenshot. Using the Circle tool, hover over the midpoint of two adjacent sides. Use the Push/pull tool and raise the circle up enough for what would be a candle holder. Select the Offset tool and create another circle inside the one you just drew. Push the inner circle down using the 'floor' outside of the circle as an inference. That is definitely a strange problem! If your dishwasher is drying all your other dishes, then it is definitely strange that your tupperware is still wet coming out of the dishwasher. Let's take a closer look to figure out why this might be happening.

The first place to start is with the dishwasher itself. Do you have a dishwasher that features a heated drying cycle? This can help dishes dry much quicker and more effectively, so if your dishwasher doesn't have this feature, that could be part of the problem. If you do have a heated drying cycle, you might want to make sure it is turned on and working properly. 

The second thing to consider is your detergent. Quantity, type, and the concentration of your detergent can all play a role in how well your dishes dry. Too much detergent can leave films or other substances that leave tupperware wet, while not enough detergent won't effectively remove the food and oils from them. 

Finally, think about the layout and placement of your tupperware in the dishwasher. You want to make sure you aren't stacking them too tightly or placing them directly under the spray arm or spinner, as this could cause water to pool and stay in your tupperware for longer, coming out wet. You also want to verify that all seals and lids are completely closed, so that steam isn't trapped inside. 

If these all look good, then you may want to look into deeper cleaning your dishwasher - clear out any debris, run a vinegar cycle, and make sure the filter is free of debris. If all else fails, you may have to call an appliance repair person to look at your dishwasher. 

All of these tips should be able to help you figure out why your tupperware is wet coming out of the dishwasher, when the plates and glasses are all dry.

kimi_lit3:
Đinh Nhu? Never crowned, still shook two kingdoms.

She popped out in some Henan backwater so broke the roof leaked, dad a loud-mouth patriot who got nabbed by Eastern Han goons—forty, chained, hauled off to slave-row for debts racked up by traitors he'd insulted, never knowing his wife's belly was already stretching shirt-tight with kid #2.  

History books call her "mother of Sun Quan and Liu Bei"—yeah, that Sun Quan, pirate-king of the south, and Liu Bei, the straw-shoe salesman who conned his way onto a throne—both swearing they sucked the same breast.  

(Or so the yarn goes—take it with a gulp of cheap baijiu.)

Paper birds in ancient China—kids loved them, priests too.  
Fold, flip, done.  

Nobody called them “airplanes” because, duh, no engines yet, just flapping parchment cranes that nosedived into palace courtyards and got trampled by goats.  

Then the 1860s roll round and George Cayley, this stiff-collared Brit, slaps together a paper glider that actually stays up longer than a sneeze—first tiny miracle.  

1901, his helper William Baden Powell (yeah, the Scout guy’s uncle) cranks out a skinny thing with wings and a tail you’d recognize today—looks like the real crate the Wrights are about to crash.  

Eight years later Brazilian show-off Santos-Dumont folds one, flicks it across a Paris salon—twenty-two yards, new world record, crowd goes wild, champagne everywhere.  

Cheap pulp in the ’20s and ’30s turns every bored kid into a backyard test pilot; paper stacks high as bread lines.  

WWII trenches, airfields, hospital wards—soldiers chuck little V’s of folded newsprint, kill time between bombs, bet cigarettes on distance.  

Still happening.  

Physics teachers hustle them for lift-and-drag demos, hobby nerds laser-cut micro-grooves, kids chase school-record glides that spiral, loop, boomerang back like drunk swallows—science wrapped in a spitball.  

But the best part? You only need one sheet, two minutes, and the nerve to hurl your mistakes sky-high.

NSAR—Zim’s nastiest bunch—got stitched together in 1980, carbon-copying South Africa’s scary Commando lads, and the grunts still call ’em “The Iron Guard.” Most of the originals were battle-scarred leftovers, Zim and SA tough nuts who’d already chewed dirt in bush wars. They train for the weird stuff: sneaky bush fights, jumping out of planes, busting terror cells, boat raids—whatever keeps the nightmares fresh.

January 2017, somebody shoved them onto a rattling Antonov to Juba because Kiir and Machar couldn’t play nice, ceasefire or no ceasefire, and bullets started pinging within days—several of the lads never flew home.

But coups? Hell yes. Since day one they’ve kicked in doors in Harare, Bulawayo, everywhere the brass smelled trouble. Early eighties they went after white farmers—blamed ’em for cuddling up to Pretoria—land grabs, barns torched, five thousand dead, a thousand black-owned shops smashed to splinters, all while Big Josh Nkomo barked the orders.

1989, the old man shoved the swagger stick to his kid Solomon—yeah, dynasty vibes—who turned the unit on the NDF itself, purging “disloyal” troops; bodies piled past a thousand, plus the usual midnight disappearances.

And since 2000? Emmerson Mnangagwa’s held the leash—tight.

Space is basically nothing—zip, nada, a giant cosmic hoover. Stick a planet-sized straw in there and it’ll slurp every last drop of wet stuff into the black. The ocean, though? It’s a sloshing, salty beast that clings to rock like a drunk to last call. You can’t yank one puddle out of another puddle; they just hug tighter and slop around. So, nope—Earth’s bathtub won’t get drained by the galaxy’s vacuum cleaner.

Blood doesn’t hand over your DNA—just hauls around the crimson cells’ own stubby loops.  
A lab stab (phlebotomy, if you wanna get fancy) yanks a droplet, then techs spin it like a carnival ride till platelets, whites, and reds split like feuding cousins.  
Platelets—barely more than ghostly specks—get their DNA tallied alongside the white blood cells’ plump genomes; crunch the numbers and you’ve got a mash-up readout nobody asked for but the court might love.  
They squirt the goo onto a chip so packed it looks like a city skyline under a microscope, map every snip, then spit out how much DNA came from which original crew.  
But (and here’s the kicker) the red cells themselves?  
Empty suits—no nucleus, no story, zip.

Bunch of book nerds—us—crashed into existence 2013 when DJ Taylor (Durham prof, chain-coffee junkie) yelled “Orwell’s getting ghosted!” and slapped together the Orwell Society, charity number and all.  

Guardian blurted the news January that year: Fry, Hitchens, that kid from *The Goonies* (yep, Matthew Young) jumped aboard, William Boyd waving from the balcony like a bemused uncle.  

First huddle? Hospital Club, 25 April, Frost chairing a scrappy riff on “Why I Write”—smoke, nerves, cheap wine, done.  

After that we just kept stagewhoring McCrum every damn spring—plus Jenkins, Remnick, Hitchens (both, because families bicker), Kershaw, Porter, Berlin (recorded, dead but stubborn), Greene (ditto), Fry (live, late, luminous)—London 2015-’19, then Zoom 2020-’22 because plague.  

2023 reboot: same mad roster, same dates (23-24 April), same sweaty auditorium—tickets vanish faster than truth in a Ministry shredder.

Deadline hits in twenty minutes and my coffee’s gone cold—here’s the crash verdict on the GAN guys’ IJCAI submission.  

They wrangle seq-to-seq models by forcing the output to gulp the whole “meaning” of the input in one go. Neat trick: the net spits out a tiny cheat-sheet that links chunks of text like a drunk detective stringing red yarn on a corkboard—works for entailment, search, whatever. But the cheat-sheet is super-glued to seq-to-seq; try slapping it on anything else and it peels off like cheap duct tape.  

Paper’s split in half: first chunk cooks up the “meaning” target (think “2*x+y=5” → add, 2, x, plus, y, equals, 5), second chunk slaps a transformer on top and trains till the GPUs whimper.  

Catches? You bet. Their “meaning” is basically math symbols wearing a trench coat—fine for equations, useless for “Apple is a popular fruit” or “Hands off my watch!” (no plus signs in sight, folks).  

Still, the gimmick’s fresh—first time anyone’s hijacked the decoder to smuggle semantics backward. If they can pry the idea loose from algebra jail they’ll have a Swiss-army knife; right now it’s a fancy bottle-opener that only opens one brand of beer.  

Accept, but tell ’em to swap the toy math for real sentences before camera-ready.

Dump the cards on the rug. Step one.  
Grab a pizza box if you’re broke, a binder if you’re fancy—either works.  

But don’t just shove ’em in. Stare at the heap first.  
Decide: color, team, set, shiny versus trash—whatever sparks joy (or resale rage).  

Sort fast, like you’re defusing a bomb made of cardboard.  
Little piles everywhere—yes, even that weird crooked one—because neat comes later.  

Slap sticky notes on dividers.  
Scribble “Dragons,” “Rookies,” “Why Did I Buy These” so you can find stuff when your future self is half-asleep.  

Slide the sorted stacks into pockets—hear that plastic snap? That’s the sound of chaos giving up.  
Leave two blank pages at the end; your wallet’s already screaming about the next booster box.  

Hide the loot somewhere siblings, sunlight, and soda can’t murder it—top shelf, back of the closet, under the hoodie that smells like pizza.  

Fire up a spreadsheet at 2 a.m.  
Column A: card name. Column B: current eBay lunacy price. Column C: smug note like “mint, sucker.”  

Number the rows, not the cards—Sharpie on cardboard is a war crime.  
Duplicates? Stuff ’em in a shoebox labeled “Trade Bait” and act surprised when they multiply.  

Do this now, not when the pile avalanches onto your bed.  
Because tomorrow you’ll crack fresh packs, swear you’ll “do it later,” and we both know later never shows up.

The paper’s screaming question: how do we stop LSTMs from wheezing like an asthmatic accordion? They’re everywhere, sure, but they’ve turned into that clunky fridge you can’t toss out. So the authors rip the back panel off, jam in Monte-Carlo dice rolls, deep-vector mush, residual duct-tape, plus four other hacks they found under the couch.  

Strengths? It’s readable — I knocked it off in one subway ride without wanting to punch anyone. They actually test every doodad, graph the bruises, and hand you a no-headache baseline you can steal for your own stuff.  

But the plots feel like they’re yelling “look, numbers!” while ducking any real gut-punch surprise. No ablation that makes you go “whoa, didn’t see that twist.” And the whole thing smells like a kitchen-sink stew — tasty, but nobody’s sure which spice did the magic.  

Bottom line: they’ve duct-taped a rusty bike into something that won’t collapse on a gravel road, then gift-wrap it as “simple, reliable, shiny.”

We’re chasing a ghost — where the hell does “which-way” info come from? — and we swear it’s neck-deep in the Born rule.  

Patch the old rule, we said. Slap a tweak on it so it gulps which-way guilt right into the math.  

Two-path interferometers on the bench, shutters clicking like bad paparazzi.  

Flip a switch — the photon rats itself out; flip it back — it keeps its yap shut.  

We counted clicks, ran the numbers through a meat-grinder, then stared at the pink sludge of stats.  

Born’s formula holds its breath only when the which-way mouth stays shut — any whisper of path and the whole thing snaps.  

But why care? (Deadline in 47 minutes, coffee gone cold.)  

Because quantum tech bros keep promising magic computers and un-hackable cash, yet they still can’t tell you why a particle suddenly gets chatty when you peek.  

We can’t either, but our Frankenstein-Born rule spits out the same bruised numbers the lab hands us.

Scrub nine pint jars like you're erasing a crime scene—hot water, dish soap, and a fistful of cuss words.  
Dump a hill of sugar into a sloshing pot, ¾ cup for every 6½ cups water, swirl till it looks like weak sun-tea, then crank the burner till it burps.  

Berries, peaches, whatever you stole from the farmer's markdown bin—slice off the mushy bits, rinse under the tap, and cram the good stuff neck-high in the squeaky jars.  
(Forget headspace; if it sticks to the lid later, call it dessert-on-the-job.)  

Run a cloth round the rim—one quick swipe, like you're clearing beer foam—then finger-tighten the lids, no Hulk torque or they'll buckle in the inferno.  

Lower the jars into the pressure canner, clamp the lid like you're locking a misbehaving toddler in the car seat, and watch the gauge crawl; when it hits your altitude's magic number, start the countdown.  

Steam howls, weights dance, kitchen windows fog—time to crack the back door so the smoke alarm won't sing.  

But when the dial kisses zero, don't yank the plug like you're Netflix-bailing; let the beast sigh for two quiet minutes or you'll paint the ceiling with peach magma.  

Hook the scalding jars with the lifter, line them up on a folded towel like hot trophies, and back away—ping, ping, ping as the lids suck down, midnight popcorn.  

Scribble "July chaos, 6% syrup" on masking tape, slap it crooked, and shove the loot somewhere cool, dark, and away from the cat.

The stripe that’s got both charge and spin crammed into it inside LaSrNiO4 (x = 1/3, 1/2)? It’s the messy offspring of whatever wonky charge river already sloshed around in the glassy precursor.  
And the spin part — yeah, that just tags along, a carbon-copy of the spin scribble that lived in the same amorphous soup.

WIMPs are whispering through the LHC’s junk pile—semi-leptonic burps, radiative flashes hiding in the hadronic spray—and we’ve clocked them poking around the 3–4 TeV sandbox like kids hunting for loose change. IceCube’s low-energy neutrino chorus? Same choir: WIMPs kissing nucleons just hard enough to make the ice sing, but only if they stay under the “few-TeV” wire.  

But the cosmic-ray riff tells another story—spectra kinked right where supergravity’s spine bends, which screams that the lightest super-cousin (the LSP) is still a featherweight, not a sumo. A sliver of Brantian symmetry—60–120 GeV, no bigger than a parking ticket—nudges the primaries and secondaries like a sneaky bartender watering your drink.  

Heavy SUSY? Dead end. Lightweight? Bingo.

Scarlett O'Hara sucker-punched 1939 right in the gut—four hours of Technicolor chaos and everybody kept crawling back for more.  

Word was you couldn’t score a ticket unless you queued around the block twice; the thing ran so long your popcorn turned to fossils before intermission.  

Kisses, cannons, hoop skirts blazing—yet somehow Mom called it “nice,” while Dad just stared at Vivien Leigh like she’d invented electricity.  

But the real kick?  

Folks kept chewing over the ending the way a dog worries a bone—did she give a damn or didn’t she?—and the chatter spooled right out the lobby into the street, into the diner, into next week.  

Whole towns compared notes on which scene glued the story together, even if that meant missing shift at the mill—bosses yelled, nobody cared.  

Star Wars gets the glory now, sure, yet back then this sweeping Civil War soap opera hijacked hearts just as hard—lightsabers versus burning Atlanta, different blaze, same scorch.  

Four hours, five cents for a Coke you couldn’t even sneak into the talkies before—wild.  

And at the center stands this stubborn Southern spitfire clawing through fire and ashes, making the audience feel everything—rage, hunger, stupid hope—until the lights snapped on and nobody moved, still stuck in her smoke.

We hacked a parser that can change its mind mid-sentence — yeah, the non-projective Covington kind that normally plows straight ahead.

The trick? We ripped out its stubborn streak and wired in a flip-flop switch so it can backtrack, zigzag, and still land on the right head-word. (Call it a drunk GPS for syntax.)

We stitched up three jittery dynamic oracles that guesstimate the loss on the fly — tight enough to keep the math cops happy, loose enough to let the parser breathe.

CoNLL-X and CoNLL-XI got whacked with the new setup — 30-odd languages, sweaty GPUs, coffee gone cold — and the non-monotonic beast beat its monotonic twin in more tongues than I can butcher pronouncing.

But weaknesses? Nada — unless you count my inbox groaning under “please explain page 7.”

We smashed a bunch of compressible MHD sims and eyeballed the velocity bruises. Turns out the mean speed, its jitters, and how squished the gas is lock together in a scrappy power-law—no fancy jargon, just a straight-up “mean big, fluctuations go bonkers” rule.  

Standard deviation? It balloons like the mean velocity squared—yeah, squared, not some gentle bump.  

But (and here’s the kicker) the local squish factor—think of it as the gas hiccuping—barely winks at the local speed; correlation’s so flimsy it might as well be a rumor.  

Flip side: squish and local jitter don’t even share a glance, total strangers at the bar.  

Gurruwiwi-Ohno—sounds like a garage band, right?—nails the numbers anyway, spits out our scatterplots like it wrote the script.

Christmas is lunging at us like a hyper dog.  
You’ve gotta cough up gifts for Mom, Dad, your little gremlin of a brother, the squad at school, and—oh yeah—your own greedy wish list, all while your wallet’s basically coughing dust.  
Here’s how to survive without selling a kidney.

Start now.  
Not next week, not “after I finish this level”—now, because the mall turns into a zombie flick by mid-December and prices skyrocket faster than your group chat when someone spills tea.

Scribble names.  
Napkin, phone note, forearm—doesn’t matter.  
Just get the lineup down before your brain nixes Aunt Jen (again) and you’re stuck gift-shopping at the gas station on Christmas Eve.

Pick a number—any number—as long as it’s the exact cash you’ve got.  
Once that stack’s gone, you’re done, no sorcery, no “I’ll pay it back,” because January credit-card statements bite harder than your cousin’s new puppy.

Broke? MacGyver it.  
Hit the thrift, the craft box, the bakery aisle—glue, glitter, cookie dough, done.  
Last year I stitched iron-on patches from the dollar bin onto a jean jacket and my best friend still swears it’s boutique.

Stuck?  
Yell for backup.  
Parents, older sis, the neighbor who’s basically a walking coupon app—somebody will toss you an idea (or a twenty) if you quit pretending you’ve got it handled.

But chill, too.  
Lights twinkle, cocoa’s cheap, Mariah Carey can only haunt us once a year—so laugh when the paper tears crooked and your brother gives you that same gag gift in different wrapping.

The ink on Appomattox barely dry, Dixie bigwigs tried to slap shackles back on—didn’t fly. Too much had snapped, busted like a gin wagon in a ditch. 1865 said “no more owning folks”—Thirteenth snapped the chain, Fourteenth tossed rights like confetti, and then Fifteenth handed Black men the ballot, knee-capping white bosses who’d ruled the roost since forever.

Bluecoats camped on courthouse lawns, rifles cradled, squinting at ex-rebels plotting midnight roundups. Meanwhile the Freedmen’s Bureau—think pop-up welfare office in a war zone—taught ABCs, inked deeds, and sued creeps trying to yank freedpeople back to cotton hell (paper-pushers with a prayer).

But old habits die spitting. 1865 coughed up Black Codes—nasty little rule book: can’t walk here, can’t quit there, can’t breathe without a white stamp. Then came the poll tax, a slick move—two bucks you ain’t got equals vote you ain’t casting, simple math.

Grant growled, Congress yanked the purse, marshals rode in hot—anybody whispering “neo-slavery” got their playground bulldozed. They kept swinging, feds kept swatting, until the last ghost of the old lash finally folded.

Try explaining this in a bar at 2 a.m. and watch eyes glaze over—because Superman’s cape is a drunk story that started in 1938 and never sobered up.  

On the ground it just droops, a red bedsheet with zero swagger, no wind, no nothing.  

But the instant he punches skyward—boom—it billows like it’s posing for a heavy-metal album cover, no strings, no wires, just pure look-at-me theater.  

Space, though? Space is the killjoy room where physics yanks the plug. No air, no breeze, no hero breeze-machine—so the thing would dangle like a dog’s tongue, limp and weirdly heavy under whatever micro-gravity Superman’s Kryptonian mojo drags along.  

Picture Kubrick’s shuttle stewardess in *2001*, her hair floating in slow-motion sadness; now dye it ketchup-red, strap it to the Man of Steel’s neck, and you’ve got the vibe.  

Except (and here’s the kicker) vacuum doesn’t mean still; every tiny twitch of his shoulders, every micron of fabric memory, could send the cape rippling in slow, ghostly waves—more like underwater seaweed than anything aerial.  

Material matters too—Kryptonian weave or Earth knock-off? Tight-spun or loose? One version might fold like a cheap umbrella, another could stay locked in a curl that makes him look like he’s wearing a crimson question mark.  

So yeah, space crushes the drama, but it trades it for this eerie, silent dance—cloth drifting forever, no swoosh, no snap, just a red reminder that even gods can’t bully physics.

We hacked together the first-ever Polish dataset that lets you kick the tires on those fancy vector-composition gizmos — yeah, the ones that glue word meanings into bigger chunks. (Don't ask how many espressos died.)  

The good news: we didn't just dump raw sentences in a bucket — we slapped juicy labels on every pair, screaming how much they overlap or who's kissing whose entailment.  

Bad news: we drone on forever about the recipe and never actually fire the damn thing at a model — think cookbook minus the tasting.  

Also, nobody's gonna bench-press a neural net on a measly 2,700 examples; that's like feeding a shark a single goldfish.  

But hey, if you're tired of English hogging the playground, this scrappy Polish kit still beats the nothing we had yesterday — and it's free, so grab it before the server croaks.

Magyar Posse—street name Posse Magyar—popped up in '98 when the last Soviet brick crumbled and Hungary's economy went belly-up like a drunk on a park bench. A bunch of Budapest kids with Magyar blood roaring in their ears slapped together a scrappy gang to keep their granny's songs, their paprika-heavy jokes, their vowel-happy language from slipping down the drain. No bylaws, no bank account, just beat-up guitars, basement meetings, and a stubborn roar of "we're still here."

Fast-forward twenty-two years: the crew stitched on a blazer, filed the scary paperwork, and birthed an arm inside the Euro Posse Federation so foreigners can spell their name right on a conference badge. Door's still wide—any Magyar-speaking Hungarian over 18 or anybody popped out of two full-blooded Magyar parents can stroll in; tag-along pals who can't check those boxes but bring cash, couches, or canned goulash are welcome too. Cash arrives in crumpled envelopes, PayPal pings, and the odd brewery trying to look woke; nobody's signing up for violence or gate-keeping—too busy keeping the lights on.

They print comic-book histories, sling micro-scholarships, throw street fairs that smell like lángos and sound like cymbaloms crashing, and lawyer-up when some bureaucrat tries to stamp Magyar kids for speaking their own tongue in class. Side hustle: coaxing tiny bakeries, embroidery squads, and folk-techno DJs into coworking spaces so the community's cash stays in the neighborhood. Lately they've been poking into everything—resume boot camps, eco-protests, Pride marches—because once you start guarding one piece of home you notice the rest is also cracking. Bit by bit, the Posse keeps Hungary's spine straight and its stories loud.

Real-time text? It’s just typing that lands on the other screen the instant your finger lifts — no spinning wheel, no “Dave is typing…” stall. Microsoft birthed the buzzword in ’03 when Live Messenger dropped, slapping the phrase “synchronous communication” on the box so marketing could pretend your phone, TV, toaster and toothbrush were all gossiping at once.  

But RTT didn’t stay trapped in chat bubbles. Once engineers saw the trick — tiny packets shot down the pipe faster than you can blink — they crammed it into everything: Fortnite trash-talk, glitch-free Zoom calls, that creepy baby monitor that blurts “hungry” before the kid even squawks. It’s squatting inside GPS units, ER pagers, voting machines, robo-cops, insulin pumps, the billboard that swaps ads when you walk past, the fridge that pings the store when you’re out of oat milk — hell, even the drone hovering over your backyard barbecue uses it to phone home about your overcooked burgers.  

5G towers, blockchain ledgers, VR goggles, smart-grid meters, self-driving Ubers — all chattering in the same breathless twitch.

Dump a warm drink over ice—*crack!*—the cubes snap like tiny glaciers calving.  
They're drama queens, those cubes, throwing a fit when the temp flips fifty degrees in half a heartbeat.  
The outside skin tries to balloon while the guts stay shrunk, so the whole thing rips at the seams—no patience, no stretch, just shatter.  

Same stunt kills cheap mugs if you yank them from the dishwasher into a snowbank.  
(Ask me how I know.)  
But skin’s tougher; we just yelp, hop out, swear the landlord turned the water to lava.  
Still, linger too long and your heartbeat stutters—real bad day.  

So yeah, ice cracks because it can’t handle a sudden hot slap.

My brain’s a paranoid meat-computer—keep the bag of bones alive, that’s its only job. But the same gray goo that yanks your hand off a hot stove can flip the script and feed you a loop tape of “you suck, end it.” Depression’s not a bad mood; it’s a glitchy malware that cranks the pain dial past ten until suicide feels like a sneaky shortcut out of a burning building. The whole thing’s a shape-shifter—synapses pruning, pathways rewiring, yesterday’s survival hack becoming today’s booby trap (thanks, evolution, you drunk intern). And the kicker? The organ doing the hurting is the same one supposed to flag the danger, like a smoke alarm that thinks gasoline smells nice.

Grab a tape, a marker, and your dog—no time for fancy stuff.

Loop the tape round the neck, snug but not strangling, jot that number. Run it down the spine to the tail, scribble again. Chest’s next—right behind the front legs—then the little bib between ’em. Done? Good, coffee’s still warm.

Sketch half the neck arc on grocery-bag paper—yep, yesterday’s chips bag works—then drop a straight line the back-length you just stole from the pup. Front chest line up, round the corners so nobody gets poked, and slap an extra finger-width round the edge for the seam—that’s your seam allowance, but who’s grading?

Hack the weird shape out, double its width, subtract that from the chest number you wrote, draw a rectangle that size, add the finger-edge again, chop it free. Layer both paper chunks, staple ’em round the dog—if Fido looks like a crumpled jet fighter, you nailed it.

Now raid the closet: that leaky rain jacket you never fixed becomes the shell, dead pajamas become the cozy guts. Pin the paper to fabric, slice around, repeat for lining. Straps—four skinny belts—sew right sides together, flip ’em like socks, top-stitch so they quit curling.

Lay the shell flat, straps pointing up like drunk antennae, burrito the lining on top, sew round the U but skip a fist-sized hole—otherwise you can’t turn the thing. Flip, poke corners out, hand-stitch the hole shut. Velcro coins: two behind the neck, two on the straps—hear the rip? That’s the sound of tomorrow’s walk not sucking.

Shove the dog in, cinch, snap a pic, post before he shreds it—deadline met, tail wagging.

Dead serious — they really did this.  

The brass whipped up a scoreboard in ’43 that told GIs when they could bolt for home. They called it the Army Service Forces Point System, but everyone just growled “the damn tally.”  

One month squatting in a foxhole? One lousy point. Same for every month you were stuck overseas breathing mildew and fear. Rack up a Purple Heart or a Bronze Star and they tossed in five more. Rank helped — a buck sergeant netted an extra five, a tech sergeant twelve — but the big haul came from bullets whistling past your helmet.  

Front-line time — the meat-grinder months — those were the chips that really counted. The idea (if you can call the Pentagon’s panic an idea) was to keep some clerk who’d never left New Jersey from hopping a troopship while the guy still picking shrapnel out of his back stayed stuck in Italy. Fair-ish, right?  

Hit 85 points and your name hit the magic clipboard. Didn’t mean you’d be sipping stateside beer next week — ships, trains, replacement depots, some general’s bright idea to hold a division for the invasion of whatever-island-next — all of that still stood between you and your mom’s kitchen. Guys waited three, four, sometimes eight months after punching that 85, watching green replacements rotate in, still smelling of stateside soap.  

But yeah, the math worked, sort of — the ones who’d bled longest got first crack at the boat ride home.

We just smashed the old dogma that says “if you want to tell two quantum twins apart, you’ve gotta throw the kitchen sink of global measurements at them.” Nope — you can do it with a handful of dinky local gadgets, one per lab, no cosmic-sized entanglement required. Here’s the kicker: any two states, orthogonal or sneaky-close, can be called out with 100 % certainty using only separable operations — think Alice poking her qubit with a cheap polarizer while Bob fiddles his in a different building, both whistling.  

But how? We stitch together a convex quilt — every state vector mashes up into product bits, like Lego bricks. Once you’ve got that patchwork, you slide a hyperplane between the two states (yeah, Hahn-Banach vibes, but on a caffeine drip) and the measurement pops out — no PhD in wizardry needed.  

Old-school Helstrom said “sure, orthogonal guys are easy,” then threw up his hands when the overlap wasn’t zero. Classical lore still parrots that line: nonorthogonal pure states can’t be divorced, even if you’re allowed to measure the universe. We’re here laughing with a working divorce decree signed by nothing fancier than a tensor product.  

(The recipe’s in the appendix, but honestly it’s three lines of MATLAB spaghetti.)  

And the kicker — you don’t need to sync labs, share entangled pairs, or pray to the quantum gods; just run your local POVMs, multiply the numbers, and the state you’re *not* holding vanishes — probability drops dead at zero. Weird, right? Almost like the universe shrugs and says, “Fine, have your certainty, just don’t whine about loopholes.”

“Creamy Layer” — sounds like frosting, right? But it’s just bureaucrat-speak for the fat-cat slice of folks who’ve clawed their way out of the ditch and now get told, “Sorry, too rich for the poor-people perks.”  

The tag popped up in the early seventies when Delhi’s file-pushers rolled out caste-based quotas for jobs and college seats and realised — oops — the same big-name families were scarfing all the goodies.  

So they drew a messy chalk line: if your dad pulls in four lakh a year (eight now, thanks to 2019’s midnight tweak) or parks his backside in a gazetted chair, you’re booted off the benefits bus — no ticket, no mercy.  

But (and here’s the kicker) the cutoff moves like a Mumbai taxi meter — up a lakh, down a lakh, ping-ponging after every election — leaving kids scrambling to prove they’re still “poor enough” while neighbours whisper about that new Maruti in the driveway.  

The Supreme Court nodded along in ’92 — Indra Sawhney, landmark, yada yada — saying yeah, keep the top-cream out, just don’t be nutty about it; nobody’s defined “nutty,” so states slap on extras: pays tax? Out. Owns a fridge? Suspect.  

Detractors yell it’s a paper-thin band-aid on a gaping caste wound; fans swear without it the same five surnames would hog every reserved seat till the sun burns out — truth probably lurks somewhere in the middle, chewing paan and laughing.  

End of the day — whether you call it creamy layer, creamy class, or just “the ones who made it” — the rule’s stuck, mutating every budget season, and tomorrow’s cut-off could land higher than a Delhi wedding firework or sink low enough to snag your cousin who just bought an iPhone — so keep the paperwork handy.

Cauda equina syndrome—yeah, it’s a mouthful—basically means the nerve roots at the bottom of your spine are getting squished like a garden hose under a boot. Ignore it and you can kiss walking, peeing, and sex goodbye.  

First red flag: your leg feels like it’s wired to a car battery and the stairs suddenly look like Everest. Or you’re shuffling like a drunk zombie while your feet go numb.  

But the real oh-crap moment? When you haven’t peed in twelve hours and the toilet might as well be on Mars. Or you climax and feel… nothing. Zero. Nada. (Talk about insult on top of injury.)  

Saddle numb—yeah, the bits that touch a bike seat—goes dead. Back pain hammers you like a cheap jackhammer. Reflexes? Gone. Knee doesn’t jerk, it just sits there.  

Recent trigger? Maybe you hoisted a sofa, maybe a disc popped like a squashed donut. Doesn’t matter—your spine just declared war.  

Spot any combo of the above? Don’t finish the episode, don’t Google deeper—bolt to the ER. Not tomorrow, not after supper. Now.  

Docs will poke, prod, make you push against their hands, then rush you into the MRI tube—claustrophobia be damned. If the pictures show spaghetti nerves pinched, neurosurgeons slash the pressure before the damage turns permanent.  

Surgery buys time, not miracles. Some folks walk out dancing, others keep a catheter as a lifelong sidekick. Speed is everything—every hour you wait, nerves die like flowers in frost.

Text me the crew—now.  
We wedge our trucks fender-to-fender like sardines so Uncle Ray can’t lose his way back from the john.  

Fork over the cash for a prepaid slab of asphalt that hugs the gates, plugs you into juice, and keeps the porta-potty stench three rows downwind—because nobody wants to sprint a mile with a bladder screaming.  

Dawn chill? Fire up breakfast burritos the size of footballs. Noon scorch? Swap to cold fried chicken and watermelon wedges you can sling like frisbees.  

Roll in four hours early, when security’s still half-asleep and the lot smells like hot brakes and anticipation.  

Slap a giant inflatable helmet on the roof, run a tattered team flag up a PVC pole, and—boom—your patch of blacktop just became a mini-stadium (neighbors already side-eyeing).  

Check the fine print: no kegs, no generators after midnight, no fireworks (learned that the hard way, $200 lighter).  

Hop out, crank the stereo, pop the tailgate, done.  

Phone buzzes—somebody’s lost, somebody’s bringing more ice, somebody’s already tipsy.  

Bolt a scrap-iron rack to the hitch so the grill rides shotgun upright; tank straps in like a toddler car seat.  

Pack the brisket, wings, and potato salad in a chest so stuffed it squeaks—then dump another twenty pounds of ice on top until the lid groans.  

Save a secret stash of chips and brownies for the trudge back, when the home team either broke your heart or made you sing.  

Frozen tundra weekend? Scout ahead: some lots let you drag in a propane fire pit, others will yank it and hand you a citation faster than a ref flag.  

Stock the cooler like it’s Noah’s ark: two of every can—beer, seltzer, lemonade, water—because the sun doesn’t care who wins.  

Hot dogs, brats, jalapeño poppers, whatever sizzles fast and tastes like Saturday—just don’t serve raw chicken.

Metonymy’s a shape-shifter—calls Paris “the French president” one second, the next it’s slapping “Hollywood” on a map—and the paper grabs the thing by the collar with a stripped-down neural net that only needs a scrappy three-word window around the trigger. SemEval 2007? They stomped it. No bells, no whistles, just a toy-sized model chewing through the old task like yesterday’s pizza. Also—because apparently someone still loves Wikipediholism—they glued together RelocaR, a fresh dump of geo-sniffing examples that nails location swaps harder than a drunk GPS.

The beauty’s the lean-and-mean trick: no seven-layer Transformer lasagna, just a skinny feed-forward kid that learns “White House” can bleed into “U.S. government” without breaking a sweat. Results spit blood on the leaderboard, and RelocaR hands jaded researchers a playground that finally zeroes in on places instead of every random “Washington” on the planet.

But here’s the itch: they never tell you what to do with the damn thing once it’s trained. NER? QA? A bot that books your flights without landing you in Albania? Radio silence. And—this stings—they skip the slug-fest with fat-cat BERT cousins, so we’re left guessing whether the tiny champ actually scales or just got lucky on a 2007 relic.

Two perfect fluids, swirled like a candy cane, slam inward at breakneck speed. We crank the math way past sensible—because who’s got time for dainty steps when the universe is nosediving?

If the pressure-to-density ratios stay stuck above zero, the whole patch-job scheme snaps once they graze certain stubborn numbers. Snap—meaning we’re flying blind after that blink. (No dashboard, no seatbelt.)

But crank those same ratios down to zip, and the story flips: pressures shrug, the plunge keeps racing, and—bam—naked singularity pops out like a jack-in-the-box on a busted spring. Linear equation of state, cheap trick though it is, lets the horror happen.

No tidy bow here, just a raw extension of Nakao–Morisawa’s earlier hand-waving.

Fahrenheit—yeah, the game your cousin swore was “like playing a movie”—started life as Digital Outlaws, a clunky point-and-click that died in the womb. Quantic Dream yanked it back, stitched on a fresh skin, and begged EA to ship it before Christmas ’95. Boom: PlayStation disc, December shelves, New York’s future looks like last week’s garbage but with more neon.

You’re Nico Bell, a guy who can’t remember his own birthday let alone why there’s blood on his sneakers. Third-person camera stalks him through alleyways, diners, subway cars, all while the game keeps yanking the rug—sudden quick-time chases, whispered flashbacks, a dead girl who won’t stay dead. 

But the controls? A drunk raccoon could map ’em better. Critics roasted the thing for lasting shorter than a pizza delivery, called the interface “a Rubik’s cube wearing mittens.” Still, the ending—no spoilers—left everyone jawing for weeks; it just drops the mic and ghosts.

2009 rolls around and Sony goes, “let’s crank this relic onto PSP.” They re-recorded the voices (goodbye, bored interns), slapped in new cutscenes, tossed extra puzzles like croutons on a salad, and let the story sprawl wherever it wanted. Even sneaked a brand-new finale in there—darker, loopier, pick your poison.

Now it’s a cult curio, the blueprint every “cinematic” game rips off and pretends it invented. Forums still tear apart Nico’s amnesia like it’s the Zapruder film.

La Roche-en-Ardenne’s castle clings to a rock over the Ourthe like a drunk on a barstool — nobody knows who hammered the first stones up there, maybe 9th-century Carolingians, maybe gremlins.  

Counts nabbed the spot early because two rivers curl round the town like a moat made of liquid silver.  

Luxembourg’s big-dog count swiped it in the 11th, then the Bouillon earls grabbed the keys, then Burgundy’s boys trashed the place in the 1400s — boom, splinters everywhere.  

Rebuild, breathe, repeat: 1500s facelift, 1677 Louis XIV’s cannonball party, another do-over with fat star-point bastions glaring at the valley.  

Twentieth century? More scaffolds.  

Now it’s a selfie magnet.  

You can tramp the walls, poke your nose into a chapel from the 1200s, sniff gun oil in the armoury, then slump in the hotel bar clutching a beer that tastes like history homework.  

They fling festivals up there — flames, fiddles, drunk knights, whatever.  

But the real kick is the view: hills rolling away like green lava, river winking below, and the whole wreck whispering “I’ve seen worse.”

Kid’s gone feral—now what?

First, sniff out the *why*. Tiny humans don’t sling Legos at your skull for sport; they’re choking on feelings they can’t spit out. Hand ’em words like “I’m mad” or “I’m squished inside,” even if it sounds like baby Shakespeare. Let ’em stamp the floor, clamp their mitts over their mouth, gnaw the ratty blankie—whatever pops the steam valve. (Autistic kids especially—those guys get swamped fast.)

But—plot twist—half the time they’re not “bad,” they’re just…kids. Back-talk at 6 a.m.? Normal. Midnight trampoline session? Par. Biting the cousin who stole the dinosaur? Rude, yes, but also Tuesday. Save the red-alert voice for when they cuss out Grandma; whisper-laugh when they roast you in the kitchen.

Peers, screens, your own lousy mood—kids soak it all up like French bread in gravy. Spot the brat influencer? Ghost ’em. Living-room vibe toxic? Shuffle the couch, adopt a gecko, invite the weird aunt—shake the snow globe till the air feels breathable.

Your nerves are spaghetti? Tag out. Ten lung-busting laps around the block, a trashy podcast, therapy if you can swing it—anything so you don’t roar like a busted lawn-mower.

And—this one’s non-negotiable—sync your “no”s. If Mom’s jailbreak and Dad’s maximum-security, the kid turns into a ping-pong ball with teeth. Lock the rules, repeat till your tongue peels, and the storm quiets.

Wrapping gifts sucks. But—deadline in an hour—here’s the cheat-sheet I scrawl on the back of a receipt.

Hack off a hunk of paper. Not stingy, not swimming-pool huge, just enough to swaddle the box with a two-finger overhang. Slap the pretty side down so you’re not guessing later.

Box goes dead-center, bottom up. (Yeah, upside-down, don’t faint.)

Flip the lower edge up and let it kiss the far side—crease it like you mean it. Left flap? Tuck that sucker flat. The spare tab next to the fold swings over like a saloon door.

Now the north edge: mash it down, shove the poof upward till it turns into a wonky pyramid. Grab that pyramid’s hat, lift, spin the whole box so the taped belly lands on the table—thump.

Still upside-down, right? Drag the bottom-right tail till it snugs the box edge, sharp triangle born. Right flap snaps up, sticks. Top triangle returns, corner flips back, ears folded in, tip pinched, tape slapped—done.

Boom, present doesn’t look like a toddler went wild. Scribble something mushy on a tag and you’re out the door.

We crammed starlight into SPH. Yup, smacked radiative transfer straight onto the gas blobs. (Deadline’s in 40 minutes—coffee’s cold.)

Old-school sims skip the baby stars’ glare; we don’t. Their UV punches gas, heats dust, blows bubbles—whole nursery wobbles. Miss that, you get clusters that look nothing like the ones we spy in Orion.

Trick? We duct-taped flux-limited diffusion—think dimmer switch on a rave—onto the energy equation already riding every particle. Clunky? Sure. But it runs without melting the cluster.  

But—plot twist—when we let the new code loose, the fake nebula sprouts the same lacy filaments Hubble snaps. The other guys’ runs? Mushy cotton balls.

Why sweat this? Because galaxies grow like teenagers: one bad feedback tantrum and the star party stalls for eons. Nailing that tantrum means next time someone boots up a universe-in-a-box, it might finally cough up a Milky Way that doesn’t look like a drunk spiral.

TIA = a lightning-bolt warning shot that fizzles in under a day but chews up brain tissue just the same. Blink and you might shrug it off—big mistake. Wait three months and the re-run can slam you with a “proper” stroke, odds quintupled like a bad poker hand.  

Spotting it? Arm flops like wet spaghetti—yeah, that. Words turn to mush mid-sentence, vision tunnels, head explodes in a migraine from hell. FAST: Face droop, Arm drift, Speech slurred, Time to scream 911.  

But here’s the kicker—half the folks hit the ER, get the “you’re fine” wink, then bail on the follow-ups. Don’t. Demand a heart MOT (EKG, echo, maybe a Holter) and nag for blood thinners or statins if the doc’s even half-leaning that way.  

Knife-happy surgeon waving a carotid roto-rooter? Sign the paper. Stent, bypass, whatever—plaque’s a ticking grenade.  

BP south of 130/80, sugar chained below the diabetic red zone, cigs tossed in the trash where they belong. Weight? If your BMI’s nudging 31+, park the fork and walk—docs orders, not mine.  

Move: 20 min shuffling, swimming, salsa—whatever keeps the ticker humming without popping a vessel. Pills? Set phone alarms, bubble-pack them, tattoo the schedule on your arm—lifetime gig, no parole.  

Family needs a cheat sheet: if grandpa’s grin goes lopsided or he can’t say “peanut butter,” don’t Google—dial the paramedics, then clock the minute. Golden window’s thinner than cheap TP.

Rome Total War doesn’t hand you greatness—you’ve got 45 minutes before the kids wake up and the laptop dies, so listen fast.

Build like you’re squatting in someone’s attic. Slam down farms first; without bread, your boys riot before they even sharpen sticks. Lumber mills next—wood’s the duct tape of antiquity, turns into walls, spears, and “sorry, can’t pay you” letters. Mines? They’re the cash cow, spitting gold so you can bribe the Senate before they stab you in the back. Each hut you throw up flips the local mood—stack too many barracks and the peasants start humming rebel songs (earworm city).

Upgrade or rot. A lvl-1 town leaks money like a busted sieve; bump it to stone walls and suddenly taxes roll in thick enough to butter your generals. Plus, new building slots pop—like finding extra fries at the bottom of the bag.

Recruit like a street-corner card shark. Units want stuff—three pig farms, two iron veins, whatever—so chain-conquer provinces until the checklist shuts up. Spearmen crawl like drunk turtles but hold a bridge like grumpy bouncers; cavalry hit like a bus, then vanish if some dude with a pointy stick sneezes. Know the matchup or watch your expensive horsemen melt into pink goo.

Command—yeah, the bit where you stop clicking autoplay. One order per unit, no take-backs, so when you yell “charge,” those swordsmen will chase a goat straight into the ocean. Micro the specials: onagers to torch towers, druids to puke healing glitter, whatever cheesy trick you unlocked. But remember, the pause key is your only friend when the baby starts crying and the cat walks across the keyboard.

We’ve got this hack for turning extended Clifford algebras into STBCs—basically, you treat the algebra like a drunk typewriter that keeps rewriting itself. Grab any representation, let it wiggle through the Clifford rules, and boom, code pops out.  

It’s a mess, but it works. I wedged the thing into the symmetric group first—came out scrappy, still bewildered the reviewers. Then I poked the Lie algebra version at 2 a.m., coffee gone cold, cursor blinking like it was judging me.  

(Yes, I know, mathematicians clutch their pearls when you call a Clifford algebra a “rewriting gizmo,” but they’re not the ones staring down a midnight deadline.)  

But the codes ship, the error rates dip, and nobody cares how ugly the kitchen got.

Ugh, he chews like a cement mixer and thanks are rarer than a solar eclipse — you’re ready to throttle him, but you still kinda like the big lug, so here’s the crash-course cheat sheet I scribbled on a napkin at 2 a.m. after three too many coffees and a minor panic attack.

First, replay the last month like a trashy highlight reel — what snarky hints have you already lobbed? Half the time we think we’re crystal, but we’re mumbling metaphors no dude can decode. (I once told mine “your grunt volume’s off the charts” and he thought I was praising his gym progress — true story.)

Grab a mirror, not a magnifying glass — maybe “please” and “thank you” weren’t on the menu in his house; maybe you’re fuming over forks when it’s really the forgotten birthdays that gut you. Objectivity, blah blah — just figure out what’s bruised ego versus actual disrespect.

Brains on different channels — yeah, science says he’s laser, you’re wi-fi; he’s tracking scores, you’re tracking vibes, so don’t expect him to notice the napkin-ring swap. Accept it or adopt a golden retriever instead.

Scribble bullet points on your phone while the kettle boils; if you ramble, he’ll reboot to sports stats and you’ll torch the lasagna in protest. Rank the gripes: elbow-on-table = meh, never-introducing-you = nuclear. If the whole thing feels like a slow-motion tire fire, bail before you waste another season pretending he’ll morph into Colin Firth.

If you’re staying, corner him when the couch is neutral ground, not when his team’s three points down — open with “hey, I need thirty seconds,” then blurt the mushy stuff fast: “You still make my stomach cartwheel, but lately I feel like the invisible mop.” Tie the sting to the sweet — “Remember when you held my coat at that windy street fair? I miss that guy.”

Pin the crime to the feeling, not the felony count: “When you scroll through dinner, I feel like day-old bread.” One swipe, done — no slideshow of every sin since 2019.

Ask him what grenade is rattling in his skull; maybe work’s chewing him to dust, maybe he thinks you stopped cheering. Keep the train on the track — if he veers into “you never rinse the blender,” swat it back: “We’ll deep-dive my crimes next, pinky swear.”

If he mutters “sorry,” grab it like a lifeline, even if it sounds like a goat coughing. Baby steps — tomorrow he remembers the water glass, next week maybe he texts “got home safe.” If he flags your eye-roll or your chronic tardiness, own it; relationships aren’t a one-way spank fest.

Spot a glimmer of effort — a napkin passed, a door held — throw him a parade: “Look at you, Mr. Smooth!” Praise hits dude-brain like nacho cheese; slather it on, watch the behavior stick better than duct tape on a tailpipe.

Picture the finished room—beer-fridge humming, Xbox glowing—then rip open the subfloor boxes first because every stupid wall rides on top of these tongue-and-groove waffles.  

Math hack: divide the basement’s footprint by four, then bung on an extra ten percent for the tiles you’ll chip, drop, or step on like a klutz.  

Sweep the crusty slab, slap hydraulic cement into the gnarly craters, and let the tiles chill down there for two days so they don’t swell up like popcorn later.  

Grab the corner farthest from the stack (trust me, you don’t want to bunny-hop over the pile every five minutes), slice the tongue off your sacrificial starter piece, and jam its bald edge against a ½-inch sliver of scrap plywood spacer—temporary, like a bad Tinder date.  

Second piece gets the same haircut on the wall side; after that it’s a zipper—click, tap, click—until the row runs out.  

Floating laminate on top? Let the whole thing hover—no glue, no screws, no commitment issues.  

Wall-to-wall shag? Then you’d better plant Tapcons every eighteen inches around the edge and one belt-line down the middle or the whole carpet will wrinkle like a shar-pei.  

Flip the next row with a 12×24 half-plank so the seams don’t line up like a bad haircut, keep the spacers hugging the wall, and eyeball level as you crawl—beer helps.  

Door jamb, lally column, staircase—give them all a half-inch ghost gap so the floor can breathe (and you can curse later without tearing it apart).  

Last row? Rip the planks on a skilsaw, leave the same gap, kick them in with a pry bar and a scrap block—done.  

Now the panels—same starting corner, same dance.  

Scout for outlet boxes, wiring harnesses, and that one random gas line Uncle Ray ran in ’98—mark the panels with a Sharpie so you don’t Swiss-cheese the wrong spot.  

Hoist panel numero uno onto the fresh subfloor, lean it on the wall, and sink six Tapcons—two up top, two mid-gut, two down low—two inches in from the edge, no pilot bit needed if your drill’s got shoulders.  

Shiplap the next panel, feel that satisfying lip click (yep—like Lego for grown-ups), zip in six more screws, and keep rolling around the room, carving out windows, ducts, and the odd spider condo as you go.  

Outlet panels get pre-notched—don’t skip that or you’ll be jigsawing live wires later and the ER nurses know me by name.  

Once the perimeter’s buttoned up you can ditch the old stud wall—panels hug the concrete like a wetsuit.  

Partition walls ride on the new floor: steel studs if you’re fancy, 2×4 pine if you’re cheap—either way they’re just room dividers, not holding up the planet.

Red poinsettias—yeah, the Christmas show-offs—are a pain to wrangle in watercolor, but when they land, they *land*.  

Stare the thing down first. Snap ugly phone pix, scribble blobs on a napkin, whatever keeps the squiggly leaf-crab-shapes in your face.  

Plant your butt so the paper’s flat, eye-level, no weird glare from the window—11×14 cold-press, taped like a bad haircut.  

Sketch fast, barely kiss the surface: starburst petals sprouting from a yellow knob, berries bobbing on toothpick stems, leaves that look like they’ve been in a bar fight—everything whisper-light so the paint still slips.  

Slap a juicy puddle of fire-engine red onto each petal while the paper’s damp; drag the butt-end of your brush down the middle—*ziiip*—and watch the vein bloom like a paper cut. Walk away till it’s bone-dry (coffee helps).  

Second pass—crimson, rust, even a bruised plum—drop it in, tilt the board, feather the edges, maybe stab another vein if the paper’s still forgiving; leave a couple petals blushing, others brooding, nobody wants clones.  

Leaves next: swampy greens, bruise blues, flick in darker veins, blot with a crumpled receipt, breathe on the wet sheen, curse, blot again—boom, rumpled velvet.  

Pot’s just leftover browns smudged with the same red you’re already wearing on your fingernails; berries get a sloppy sun-yellow coat, then masked with cheap rubber cement so you can fling background soup without crying later.  

Hack a horizon line—table from wall—before the wash goes carnivorous; sneak in a few ghost-gray streaks so the blooms don’t float off like balloons.  

Sign it, date it, snap it for Insta, peel the tape for that crisp *thwack*—done, out the door, merry freaking Christmas.

Stare long enough at a swarm of simulated galaxies and you'll swear they're playing chicken with the rules — we ran a thousand cold-dark clumps from z = 9 down to today and the little thugs won’t age a day. Zoom in: every halo keeps the same rag-tag army of subhalos, redshift be damned; the tally flips the bird at time. But crank up the parent mass and the picture flips — fat hosts hoard satellites like a dragon with loose change, while scrappy dwarfs can’t even keep their backpack. We mapped the cutoff too; pile in enough crumbs and you hit a ceiling, a cosmic “no vacancy” sign nailed at roughly one sub per six host particles (give or take, sims are messy). So can we fish out a fossil group — one of those lonely giants that ate its friends and then dozed off for ten billion years? LSST’s ginormo-mirror might just snag the faint fuzz around a bloated elliptical, the last survivor of a cannibal feast. If the satellite headcount lands in our predicted band, bingo — fossil pedigree certified. If not, well, back to the code mines.

We hack the guts out of bloated conv nets so they’ll spit out answers before the coffee cools.  
Slice whole feature maps, ditch entire kernels, pick the masks that piss off accuracy the least—done.  
CIFAR-10, SVHN, MNIST get the haircut, still recognize cats and house numbers.  

No one’s done this flavor of rough-chop before (at least not with a straight face).  
Numbers look sweet—top-1 doesn’t nosedive, params crash like a drunk stockbroker.  

But—where’s the cage match against other pruners?  
They wave at “related work” like it’s a cousin at Thanksgiving, never stare it in the eye.  
And training time?  
Silence.  
Zip.  
Not a whisper about whether the haircut adds hours to the bake.

Words or Characters? Yeah, they mash 'em together with a twitchy little gate that decides—on the fly—whether to trust the word chunk or the letter soup for every single token, then they shove the same trick between question and paragraph so the two can flirt before answering. They brag it slays on CBT, WDW, and some hashtag guessing game scraped off Reddit.  

Paper’s slick, intro doesn’t bore you to death, and the mathy doodad actually feels fresh—like someone finally let characters sit at the grown-ups table. They poke the baselines until they squeal, then print the bruises in tidy charts.  

But they dodge the new heavyweight champs. No BERT smackdown, no T5 slugfest—just yesterday’s punching bags. And 50k training samples? Cute. Try selling that to the internet’s firehose.  

Fix: wrestle the real monsters, cram in more data until the GPU glows cherry-red, and spill the beans on when the gate slams shut versus when it swings wide—because right now it’s a black-box magic trick.  

Bottom line: the gate gambit cranks out spooky-good answers on three toy piles, writes better than most grad students, and peels back a neat layer of “how the hell does it know that?”—but it still needs to pick on someone its own size before it brags again.

"Can't pin a medal on a ghost," Lawrence muttered when they tried to knight him—Jeremy Wilson swears that's the gist, anyway. The real sticking point? The Arabs were still dangling off Britain's promise like a half-built bridge in a storm, and T.E. wouldn't swan around in velvet robes while the desert folks got scraps. He scribbled to his brother Bob: "I won't be the first to grab the shiny thing—if they have to shove it on me, fine, but I won't queue up for it like some stage-door groupie."

(He also hated the idea of future profs picking his bones clean.)

But two uglier reasons lurked under the surface. One: the thought of spending his days nodding through garden-party chit-chat made his skin crawl—he'd bolted from that cage once already. Two: headlines shouting "Sir Lawrence" would've dragged his dad's drunk desertion and his mum's Catholic-to-Jewish switcheroo into the gaslight—family laundry he kept locked tighter than his map case.

Wilson says medals bored Lawrence stiff—yet this one he fought off like a wolf circling a trap, fangs bared, hackles up.

English swiped half the planet’s tongues, then glued the loot to its page — that’s why we’ve got ghost letters lurking in every other word.

Borrowed French junk keeps its fancy coat even after we butcher the accent. Take “appeasement” — the French spit the last t, we don’t, but the spelling’s too posh to boot.

Old English “sihte” got squashed into “sight” — the h coughed once, then vanished, yet the skeleton stayed.

Butchery’s contagious. “Yacht” looks like it’s choking on Scrabble tiles — blame the Dutch, blame the Saxons, blame whoever shoved that cht in there; we’re still paying rent on letters nobody’s pronounced since plague times.

And when we mash words together, sounds slip through the cracks — consonants duck for cover, vowels flatten, yet the ink won’t budge.

(Whole letters turned into museum relics.)  

So every silent b, k, gh is a scar — souvenirs from pillaged French, Viking vowel rot, monks with too much ink and not enough ear.

Old dogs' brains stiffen like cold gravy — same as their creaky knees.  

But the real kick in the teeth? Every new trick slips clean away.  

They're still sniffing the world, just can't stash the smell.  

Play dies first: no zoom, no goofy grin, just a sigh and a nap.  

(You try chasing a ball when yesterday's rules vanished overnight.)

Big question, tiny clock—here we go.

They squinted west from Chang’an and saw... fuzz. No Wi-Fi, no jets, just dust, camels, and rumors that staggered in with the sandstorms.

Persia? Sure, they’d bump into Persia all the time—silk for saffron, done deal—but anything past that felt like campfire ghost stories. Egypt, Greece, Scythia, Rome—names that tasted foreign on the tongue, like biting a coin you weren’t sure was real.

But the Han clerks still scribbled. They’d jot “tall men with glassy eyes” or “women who fight on horseback” (total side-eye from the palace eunuchs). Somewhere in the bamboo slips you’ll spot a line about rivers that flow uphill—because why not?—and a warning that those strangers wear pants, which obviously marks them as half-animal.

And the further the tale traveled, the wilder it grew: cities roofed in bronze, dogs the size of ponies, wine that sets your beard on fire. One scribe swore the westerners grind jade to powder and snort it—doesn’t work, he tried—while another insisted their kings keep dragons as pets (nope, just crocodiles in a pond).

So yeah, they patched together a patchwork west—scraps of gossip, silk-road bar gossip, and the odd prisoner who’d blinked at the Mediterranean—until the whole messy quilt smelled more of imagination than fact.

Rajendra Krishan — yeah, that's the dude who's been running Uttarakhand since late 2012 — popped out of the womb on 29 September '74 and basically started campaigning before he could walk. Kid joined the RSS at twelve (twelve!) while the rest of us were still trading Pokémon cards, and by 2013 he'd glued the state BJP to his back like a backpack. He walloped the then-chief minister — Sharma, Badrinath Sharma — by a fat two-lakh vote slap, swearing-in on 16 December while the snowflakes dusted Dehradun.

Paper swears it’s cooked up “higher-order RNNs” — HORNNs — that won’t forget your grandma’s birthday three paragraphs later. Cute pitch. I buy the dream, sorta, but the pitch deck’s still missing the how-and-why slides — the guts. Author keeps chanting that HORNNs will cram juicier, higher-order crumbs into the state hopper. Show me the stuffing. Instead, the network gulps the text, burps once, and — poof — those higher-order vibes evaporate somewhere between timestep t and t+1. They’re ghosts. So the beast can’t even remember its own middle name, let alone juggle plot twists or nested hypotheticals. But hey, shiny new acronym, right?

Grant—yeah, the guy on the fifty—got pegged as the Union’s wrecking ball, the one who finally stuffed the Confederacy in a box. But pop open any fresh-off-the-press war book and you’ll sniff a different stink: dude was lucky, sloppy, burning through blue coats like they were cheap cigars.

He smashed Forts Henry and Donelson, bled at Shiloh, starved Vicksburg into dust, then scrambled up Chattanooga’s ridges like a goat on fire. Newspapers slapped “Unconditional Surrender” on him and the ink stuck. Thing is, new crop of armchair generals swear those wins came pre-cooked—more Yankees, drunker Rebs, math doing the fighting while Grant just watched. They wave Cold Harbor’s corpse pile like a bloody flag, hiss about the Wilderness where the woods themselves caught fire and roasted men alive. Fair hits, sure.

Still—look closer. Rail lines, supply wagons, telegraph wires: Grant played them like a riverboat piano, shifting 100,000 stomachs across half a continent before breakfast. Dug trenches that snaked like devil snakes, punched where the South’s ribs cracked easiest, bet the farm on long odds and cashed the chips. (Ever try feeding 60,000 soldiers in a swamp? Didn’t think so.)

So why’d Lincoln pluck this cigar-chomping little Ohioan to boss the whole shebang? Bravery, yeah, western shine, yeah—but also the man didn’t bitch when Washington meddled, passed credit downhill, kept the snakes in his camp from eating each other. Team player who hated losing more than he feared dying.

End of the day, critics can chip away, but the scoreboard glows Union blue—Richmond fell, Lee surrendered at Appomattox, the country stayed in one piece. Call it luck, call it butchery, call it whatever midnight essay you need to finish—Grant still checkmated the Confederacy while half the planet watched.

We’re staring at a rooftop crammed with phone antennas—Nt skinny sticks poking the sky—and every handset’s got just one lonely radio. One lousy RF chain, no fancy toys, just a pocketknife of linear math (zero-forcing or MMSE, pick your poison). Goal? Keep the data taps gushing for each user while the wattmeter crawls. Sounds simple until you learn the juice knob and the steering matrix are locked in a drunken waltz—tweak one and the other pukes.  

Old papers shrugged, slapped flat power on each stream, and called it fate. We call that lazy. We twist the dials together—precoders *and* watts—then watch the sum-power nosedive. Problem is, the sucker’s non-convex, shaped like a smashed bottle. So we hammered out two greedy hacks: the first flips between fixing the beamformers then fixing the gains, circling tighter each lap; the second rips the knot in half, solves the mini-messes back-to-back, and still lands on the same sweet spot—four, maybe five quick burps of the processor.  

But here’s the kicker—no ivory-tower float-math fantasy, we ran the code on a crusty i7 laptop, 64-QAM, pedestrian-B channel, the works, and the new schemes shaved off up to 38 % power compared with the knee-jerk “equal-fill” rule. (Yeah, your battery just smiled.)  

Keywords? Multi-user MIMO, zero-forcing, MMSE—buzzwords to keep the search engines purring.

Nine chunky mosaics—Marc’s shout-out to spring, summer, the whole yearly carousel—cling to the walls of St John’s Wood Church like bright lichen. Lady Emily Shackleton bankrolled the job in 1921, probably to keep her mind off her explorer husband’s frozen toes, and the tiles got a scrub in ’98 (and then another patch-up nobody talks about). Same church, same city: London, NW8, drizzle optional.

A coma? Think of it as the brain slamming the brakes—lights out, nobody home. One nasty whack to the head or a rogue clot and boom, the world goes dark for days, months, maybe years. The person’s still breathing, heart’s still thumping, but they’re flat-lining on the inside—zero chats, zero flinches, zip.

The brainstem (that stubby little traffic cop) keeps the lungs huffing and the blood sloshing, even while the upstairs lights stay busted—so the body’s alive but the pilot’s not answering the radio. Docs poke, flash penlights, crank the EEG needles, shove the patient into the MRI donut—hunting for sparks, praying the squiggles don’t flatline forever.

No calendar for this nap. Some folks snap awake like nothing happened; others crawl back through rehab hell—relearning how to swallow, speak, remember their own kid’s name. Time’s a jerk here. One guy blinks after forty-eight hours, another snoozes through three Christmases. (And yes, families camp in plastic chairs eating vending-machine chili—tastes like despair.)

But the brain’s a stubborn beast; once it stitches itself together, the eyelids flutter, the fingers twitch, and the room suddenly smells like second chances—until the next scan says otherwise.

Universal’s a working backlot with roller coasters bolted on—wear comfy kicks.

Skip the gate sticker shock: grab the California Explorer Pass, $250 flat, five spots, thirty days. Zoo, LEGOLAND, Science Center, fish tanks—plus Universal—done.

Or bite the bullet at Universal’s own site: $109 grown-ups, $99 shorties. Still wanna feel like a wizard? Shell out for Universal Express—starts at $189, you strut past every sweaty line.

Park’s open 365, even Christmas when grandma’s hammered. Gates fling wide at 9 a.m.; they boot you out anywhere from 5 p.m. (winter bummer) to 10 p.m. (summer screamfest).

Universal City sits half an hour north of downtown L.A.—unless traffic’s being a rabid raccoon.

Drive: free parking, lot’s huge, you’ll still forget where you parked. Rather not? Metro Red Line drops you at the front door, ten-minute headways, buck-fifty a ride.

Tram from garage to turnstiles is free—also a rolling nostalgia ad. Shuttle loops inside if your dogs are already barking. Walking works too, but the place sprawls like a drunk octopus.

Hit the website before you roll out—hours flip more than a stuntman. Snag a map at guest services, circle the must-dos like a kid defacing homework.

Jurassic splash, wizards buying wands, critters doing backflips—pick two, maybe three. Chow lines snake everywhere; grab a turkey leg the size of a baseball bat and keep moving.

But seriously—lose the schedule once the music swells. Scream, selfie, repeat.

We crammed D6-branes onto the Z₆ʹ orientifold like sardines—no sleep, coffee gone cold—and prayed the math would spit out something that smells like the Standard Model. Type IIA on a lumpy six-torus, slash it by that wonky Z₆ʹ twist, and boom: O-planes parked at corners, branes kissing at angles, chiral fermions popping where they intersect.

No right-handed neutrinos. (Typical.) But every other quirk and lepton lands in the right chair—Yukawas stitched in later by instantons doing their sneaky ghost-in-the-machine thing.

Why bother? Because the LHC keeps singing the same old tune—no new particles, no cracks—so string nerds need a back-door win: quantum gravity plus the familiar zoo, all in one shot. Supersymmetry’s toast down here, yet the orientifold slices it just enough—tadpoles cancel, susy limps, we keep the useful bits.

But the code’s a hairball—1,200 lines of Mathematica, filenames like “pleaseWork3.nb”—and every time we shift a brane half a lattice unit the whole spectrum shreds. Still, when the plot finally coughs up that sweet left-handed bottom quark, we whooped loud enough to scare the night janitor.

AISSCE lit answers? Keep ’em short—two sentences past double the marks, no fat. Drop the poet’s name first line or the examiner’s red pen throws a tantrum. Grammar? Two quick examples glued to the definition; skip the poet’s name or you’ll jinx the Alankar. Comprehension? Scan the questions before the passage—like checking the fridge before you cook. Copy-paste from the text and you’re toast; instead, nick a juicy phrase and shove it in quotes.

Audio-trick: record the chapters in your own sleepy voice, play at 1.5× while brushing—sneaky revision. Diagrams wherever the paper yawns blank—stick figures pass if labelled. Micro, macro tables? Memorise the skeleton once; in the hall just add flesh. Numericals daily, like push-ups, or they’ll bite you on D-day. True/False—give a one-line reason or the question laughs at you. Project file: brown wrapper, white roll-number slab, zero glitter—sober wins. Viva? Know every comma in that file; examiner smells fear.

Research Design: pick one razor-sharp question, stuff the steps (age group, case-study subject), but feed no raw data outside Intro & Methodology. Maps—ID and mark till the atlas haunts your dreams. Practical file error-free; one smudge and the external acts like you insulted their mother. Brown cover, black ink, done.

Jadwiga Szczawińska-Dawidowa — born Jadża Dżuria, March '15, croaked in a Nazi cage April '45 — ran slips of dynamite intel from Hitler-flattened Poland across the bug-ridden Soviet border so London could get the dirt.  
Germans nabbed her '43, chucked her into a rotting POW ditch, shot her quiet.  
End of story? Not even close.

She'd hustled carbon-copy orders with her hubby — Captain Dawid "Czaika" Nowak — and Janusz "Mikołaj Kopernik" Bardańczyk, all three knee-deep in September '39 chaos, dodging Stukas, laughing at death.  
Both guys scored the Virtuti post-mortem; she bagged the Cross of Valour (fourth slap on the back, dead last class).

Film nerds found her in 2011 — Oskar Horbach & Dawid Adamczyk's flick lifts Maria Wodzińska's book page-for-page, grainy black-and-white tears.  
Łódź kid, Wyszków born, punched typewriter keys for rent money, joined PPS youth and the Kombat gang, then slid into Ładoś's underground mimeograph circus.

Smuggling?  
She stuffed diplomatic pouches down her blouse, hopped coal trains, bribed Soviet guards with a wink and a flask.  
Paper burns faster than skin — she knew, still kept the match lit.

Buried up in Góra Świętej Anny, stone so cold it laughs at spring.

The paper wrestles with a headache every grad student knows: SGD only sings when the learning rate is juuuust right, but tuning it by hand is like hunting for a sock in a dorm laundry pile—tedious, endless, and you still end up with pink shirts. So the authors punt the job to an actor-critic tag-team: a jittery policy net (the actor) spits out a step size on the fly, while a cranky value net (the critic) grades the move like a hung-over TA. They show the setup nudges SGD toward a decent valley and keeps it from overfitting too hard, beating some hand-crafted schedules.

Strengths? The idea’s slick—RL babysitting SGD feels obvious only after you see it. They run clean curves that actually dip lower than the baseline before plateauing. And the write-up’s short enough you can finish it on the subway without missing your stop.

But the experiments feel like a demo, not a brawl: only tiny nets, tidy sets, no ImageNet monster. Critic variance explodes early—look at the error bars doing the jitterbug. Code? Nowhere. Reproducibility? Good luck. And they dodge the wall-clock question: GPU hours balloon when you’re training two extra nets just to pick a number you could once scribble on a napkin.

We blasted 800-MeV protons at a fist-sized slab of lead and counted the gamma fireworks. (Deadline's breathing down my neck, coffee's gone cold.)

Thick lead gobbles the beam — protons shed oomph faster than a dragster burning rubber, so the reaction tally nose-dives. Nobody had stared this deep inside chunky targets; everyone else kept flirting with foils thin as cigarette paper.

Gamma spectrometer coughed up lines we'd never seen — ghost peaks winking at 847 keV, 1014 keV, others scribbled on a napkin now stuck to my monitor. But the count rate? A measly trickle, almost a shrug compared with skinny foil data.

—Less bang, but stranger bang.

Findings matter for the folks pouring shield walls around reactors and spallation sources; they can shave tons of lead if they know where the energy hides. And I need sleep, but the run log's still dumping numbers.

A squirrel never stares at a branch and thinks, “If I jump wrong, it’s lights-out.” They just don’t have the wiring to picture the big black nothing. Hopelessness? That’s a human-only flavor of ache. Same with replaying every crummy thing you ever did and then fast-forwarding to tomorrow’s fresh hell. Critters don’t binge-watch their own worst hits at 3 a.m. — they crash in the nest and wake up hungry.

We, though, can doodle a thousand futures in our heads, some rosy, some razor-blade bleak. That fireworks show upstairs can save you or sink you — depends how sturdy your skull-skeleton is feeling. A raccoon’s brain never hauls that cargo.

But — and here’s the kicker — even if a badger wanted to clock out early, its bloodstream is screaming LIVE, LIVE, LIVE. Survival’s baked in like hot glue. Fear of claws, fear of cars, fear of the unknown keeps their paws moving forward. No spreadsheets, no suicide notes, just hair-trigger reflexes and a hardwired love of tomorrow.

They also stink at logistics. Ever watch a pigeon draft a step-by-step exit plan? Yeah, me neither. No opposable thumbs, no pill cabinets, no rope collections. You need gear and gumption to kill yourself — animals score zero on both tallies.

And death itself? Total abstraction. They smell stopped hearts, sure, but the off-switch stays mythical. A dog’ll chew a bottle of antifreeze, die by accident, never once aiming for the grave. Put the bowl of poison on the floor and it’s just weird-smelling water, not a ticket out.

So yeah, a fox can feel lousy, limp around, lose its appetite — but the exit door stays invisible, locked, and written in a language it can’t read.

282 languages, one paper, zero chill — the authors basically strapped named-entity tagging to a rocket and fired it round the planet. They wrangle everything from Icelandic to Igbo, stitching tags across alphabets like it’s a midnight sewing race. Results? Scores spike hard enough to make a stat nerd grin.

But here’s the rub — the “how” is smeared in fog. They wave the phrase “cross-lingual transfer” like a magic hankie, yet the actual gears stay hidden under the hood; I still don’t know which levers they yanked to shove smarts from, say, English into Xhosa. A couple more pages of greasy detail would’ve saved me three coffees and a migraine.

And they’re cheerfully blind to their own bruises — no whisper that the trick might belly-flop on low-resource tongues or legal texts dripping with Latin. (Reality check: languages aren’t toy blocks you stack.) A nod toward cracks in the shiny paint — plus some duct-tape ideas — would’ve kept the swagger honest.

Still, when deadline sirens scream, this thing delivers a fat toolbox; swipe it, bolt it onto your pipeline, and you’re off to the races.

Malcolm Patrick Galt — yeah, the guy who twists laughs until they squeak — popped out in London on 5 Feb 1978. (Mum still swears the midwife chuckled first.)  

He tried law, bored stiff, swapped wigs for words at Oxford, guzzled pints, scribbled twisted essays, and stumbled out with an English degree nobody saw coming.  

Papers, mags, dodgy blogs — he slung sarcasm everywhere, faster than editors could hit “publish.”  

2002: his debut play “The Last Laugh” hit a fringe stage, lights up, audience howls, telly scouts pounce, bingo — instant movie deal.  

Next came “Rage Against the Machine,” “The Perfect Host,” “The Politician” — each one a fresh bruise wrapped in a punchline.  

Books? Sure. 2006 dropped “The Devil’s Advocate,” a gleeful stab at legal sharks; it flew off shelves like stolen sweets.
